processing: A pan-fired (chao qing) green tea, fixed and dried without oxidation and shaped into tight, fine strands.
harvest_season: Spring, in mid to late April, picked as one bud with two leaves in the early morning.
appearance_dry: Tight, fine strands with a little white down, likened to threads of rain.
appearance_liquor: Clear and bright, a pale yellow-green.
appearance_wet: Tender bud-and-two-leaf sets in fresh green, as is usual for a spring pan-fired green of this picking.
taste_profile: Mellow, full and fragrant, and it holds up over several infusions; the third is said to be the best.

brewing.notes: Sturdier than a bud-only green, so water a little hotter than for a delicate tea is fine. Do not give up on it early: later steeps are the point.

vintage_note: As with other Chinese pan-fired greens, it is sold as the current spring's harvest and is best drunk within about a year. Production is small, so ask for the picking date and the place when you see it.
description:
Jinshan Shiyu is a pan-fired green from Shangjinshan, a village next to Shangzhuang in Jixi county, Anhui, best known outside tea circles as the home town of the scholar Hu Shi. The name means timely rain on Golden Mountain, and the fine strands are said to look like threads of it.

The gardens sit on slopes at roughly 600 to 900 metres. Pickers take one bud with two leaves in the morning, in mid to late April, and the leaf is pan-fired into tight strands with a little down on them.

In the cup it is mellow and fragrant, clear and bright. It is known for lasting well, with the third infusion often named as the best, so give it time instead of judging it on the first steep.

This is a small local tea, and you will rarely see it abroad. Buy the current spring, and treat a very cheap bag with the name on it with some caution, since few people can check where it came from.
history:
Accounts differ on the start. One version gives the original name as Jinshan Mingwu and dates it to the Daoguang reign of the Qing, with tribute status; another places its development in the late Qing, followed by a period when it was lost.

The better documented thread runs through Wang Yutai, a tea house with roots in Jixi. It sold the tea as a Jixi speciality and is recorded as offering Jinshan Shiyu as tribute for the Empress Dowager Cixi's sixtieth birthday in 1894, to high praise. It reportedly reached Hong Kong and Singapore in the early Republican years, and production resumed in 1978.
